matchdb

A disambiguation database for nonprofit record linkage: every name and address the IRS and 990 filers have recorded for each EIN, with its source, normalized once and compiled on demand into the reference frame that npmatch matches against.

It is not a matching engine. Blocking, comparison, vetoes, scoring and tiering live in npmatch.

Install 

remotes::install_github("Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/matchdb@v0.1.1")  # the current release
remotes::install_github("Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/matchdb")         # development version

The current release is 0.1.1, git tag v0.1.1. It pairs with npmatch 0.1.1 and normalizer signature v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e, which the published database, bundles and tranches were built with. See NEWS.md. Pin it, in renv or with @v0.1.1, for anything that should reproduce results from before the normalizer moves into npnormalize.

The development version takes the normalizer from npnormalize and only suggests npmatch. Install npmatch too to match against a reference:

remotes::install_github("Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/npmatch")

Quick start: download a reference and match

Getting started walks through a full example: matching four grant recipients, reading the results, and looking at the cases that are not clear-cut.

Four references are published, built from the database. Downloading one needs no AWS account.

label EINs names rows
active-legal current BMF legal, DBA 2.75M
active-observed current BMF legal, DBA, aliases written by 2+ filers 2.89M
unified-legal every BMF release legal, DBA 4.98M
unified-observed every BMF release legal, DBA, aliases written by 2+ filers 5.14M 
library(matchdb)
b <- md_reference("active-observed", fetch = "missing")   # ~260 MB, once

m <- npmatch::np_cascade(my_query, b$reference,
                         name_freq = b$name_freq, token_idf = b$token_idf,
                         ref_index = b$ref_index)

Each bundle is checked against the md5s it was published with and against the installed normalizer (npnormalize’s signature). A stale or altered bundle is refused.

Look up an organization

With the database downloaded (md_fetch_db(), about 10 GB):

md_lookup("53-0196605")    # entity, names, addresses, events, relations, clusters, ...
md_cluster("53-0196605")   # its families: group ruling, Schedule R system, shared site, ...

Compile your own slice

A reference is described by a spec with these settings:

  • layers: which EINs.
  • name and address classes: which strings.
  • sources: who reported them.
  • corroboration: how many filers must agree on an alias.
s <- md_spec(layers = c("bmf_active", "bmf_inactive"),
             names = c("legal", "dba", "observed"),
             addresses = c("mailing", "observed"),
             min_corroborators = 2)
r <- md_compile(s)         # r$reference, r$name_freq, r$token_idf, r$report

You don’t need the whole database for this. The database is also published as parquet files split by layer and class, and md_fetch_tranches() downloads only the files a spec needs:

md_fetch_tranches(s)       # only these layers and classes, once
con <- md_tranche_db()     # a connection md_compile(), md_publish() and md_lookup() take
r <- md_compile(s, con)
md_db_close(con)

md_tranches(s) shows what a spec will download before you fetch it. Every fetch, compile and publish is logged in your matchdb folder: md_log() lists them, and md_status() says what is there now. md_tranche_diff() shows what a new release changes. See vignette("workspace").

The articles explain each choice: layers, sources, corroborators.

What is in the database

Built from pinned versions of the IRS Business Master File, 990 e-file headers, Schedules I, R and C, Form 1023-EZ approvals, the 990-N e-Postcard, the automatic-revocation list, Part VII officer name keys, and NCCS address history and geocodes. That gives 4.24M EINs, 12.8M name rows and 22.0M address rows. Relations between EINs and typed clusters are built on top.

dev/build-matchdb.R rebuilds it from scratch in about 70 minutes. dev/PLAN.md is the design, and dev/PROCESS.md records the verification gates.
